title: The Number of Ways to Make the Sum
summary: Given an integer n, calculate the number of ways to achieve the sum n using an unlimited supply of 1, 2, and 6 value coins, and exactly two 4 value coins.
statement: Given an integer n, calculate the number of ways to achieve the sum n using an unlimited supply of 1, 2, and 6 value coins, and exactly two 4 value coins. The result should be modulo 10^9 + 7. The order of the coins does not affect the count.
constraints: Coins valued one, two, and six are unlimited; at most two coins valued four are available.
Count unordered coin multisets summing to n, modulo 1,000,000,007.
hints: Separate the bounded four-valued coin from the three unlimited denominations.
Compute ordinary combination DP for coins 1,2,6, then choose zero, one, or two fours and look up the residual.
ways[0]=1; loop coins then totals ascending; return ways[n]+ways[n-4]+ways[n-8].
Coin-first DP counts unordered multisets once, and the three disjoint four-coin counts exhaust the bounded choices.
editorial: Coin-first DP counts unordered multisets once, and the three disjoint four-coin counts exhaust the bounded choices.

tests.explanation: Using no four gives 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, or 2+2; using one four gives the fourth way.
Count unlimited-coin ways for residual sums eight, four, and zero, corresponding to zero, one, or two four-coins.
